study_identification_part.si4_title: Heterogeneity of morphometric similarity networks in health and schizophrenia

study_characteristics_part.sc1_study_objective: This study applied longitudinal normative modeling to regional morphometric similarity for the first time in a longitudinal sample of individuals with schizophrenia, aiming to: (1) assess whether decreases in morphometric similarity are consistent across individuals with chronic schizophrenia; (2) measure individual deviations from normative norms at baseline and follow-up, categorizing them as infra-normal, normal, or supra-normal; and (3) assess the change over time in the total number of infra- or supra-normal regions for each individual.

rci8_quality_checking.detail: Euler number threshold: subjects with maximum absolute within-dataset centered Euler number >10 were excluded (29 subjects removed). Clinical sample: extensive visual and non-visual QC procedures including PCP quality assessment protocol metrics (signal-to-noise ratio, contrast-to-noise ratio, Foreground to background Energy Ratio, percent artifact Voxels, and Entropy Focus Criterion); ENIGMA criteria for outlier threshold defined as [mean - (2.698 × SD)]; calculated whole brain mean cortical thickness, total cortical surface area, total white matter volume, total gray matter volume, subcortical gray matter volume, and intracranial volume; summed number of outliers over all measures and designated those above mean + (2.698 × SD) threshold as outliers.
rci8_quality_checking.supporting_text: Subjects were removed if the maximum, absolute, within-dataset centered Euler number was larger than 10, and 29 subjects were removed. For the clinical sample, we applied extensive visual and non-visual image quality control procedures as described in refs. 22,23. Briefly, the non-visual quality control procedures included calculating measurements based on the ones proposed by the PCP quality assessment protocol: signal-to-noise ratio, contrast-to-noise ratio, Foreground to background Energy Ratio, percent artifact Voxels, and Entropy Focus Criterion. Following ENIGMA criteria, we defined the threshold for outliers as [mean-(2.698 × SD)]. Next, for each scan, the whole brain mean cortical thickness, total cortical surface area, total white matter volume, total gray matter volume, subcortical gray matter volume, and intracranial volume were calculated. Then, we summed for each image the number of outliers over all measures and calculated the mean + (2.698 × SD) for the number of outliers over the whole sample and designated those above the threshold as outliers.

rci9_site_effect_handling.detail: Scanner included as a categorical predictor variable in warped Bayesian linear regression (BLR) with likelihood warping; scanner-specific Gaussian noise terms (ε_s) incorporated in the model to account for scanner-specific heteroscedastic variance; per-dataset stratified splits using createDataPartition function from caret R package preserved scanner distribution across training and test splits; B-spline basis expansion (spline order=3, number of knots=5) applied to covariates. The supplement also mentions an analysis with ComBat harmonization was performed to assess replicability.

caa6_deviation_metric.answer: Z-score; categorized as infra-normal (z ≤ -1.96), normal, or supra-normal (z ≥ 1.96); total outlier count per participant (number of regions with |z| > 1.96); z-diff for longitudinal change
caa6_deviation_metric.reason: The paper explicitly defines deviation metrics including z-scores calculated from the normative model predictions, categorical thresholds for defining infra-normal and supra-normal deviations, and methods for quantifying total outlier counts and longitudinal changes.
caa6_deviation_metric.supporting_text: For each individual deviation (z) scores, quantifying individual deviation from the normative range, were calculated for all brain regions (r) and all participants (n), as follows: where y_nr means the true morphometric similarity value and ŷ_nr is the predicted mean morphometric similarity value. The difference in these values is normalized to account for two different sources of variation; (i) σ²_r, which is the aleatoric uncertainty and reflects the variation between individuals across the population, and (ii) the epistemic uncertainty, σ²_r, which accounts for the variance associated to modeling uncertainty introduced by the model assumptions or parameter selection. z-scores were then categorized as either: (i) normal, i.e., within the normative range of variation for healthy individuals with the same age range, sex, Euler number, and scanner; (ii) supra-normal: significantly exceeding the normative range; or, (iii) infra-normal: significantly below the normative range. As per previous studies, we considered a z-score ≥ 1.96 as supra-normal and a z-score ≤ -1.96 as infra-normal. [...] Differences in z-scores over time by region are calculated by implementing the z-diff approach, which takes into account the typical variation over time.

In order to replicate the findings by ref. 11, averaged z-scores of the seven functional networks were compared between healthy controls and individuals with schizophrenia at baseline using Welch t-tests. clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa8_key_findings_brief:

clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa9_key_findings_detailed:
Answer: Cross-sectional findings at baseline: The schizophrenia group showed significantly reduced morphometric similarity z-scores in the default mode network (DMN) compared to healthy controls (d=-0.36, p<0.001 FDR-corrected) and significantly increased z-scores in the somatomotor network (d=0.30, p<0.01 FDR-corrected). At follow-up, the DMN reduction persisted (p=0.041) but did not survive multiple comparison correction. Individual deviation patterns: The percentage of individuals with infra-normal or supra-normal regional morphometric similarity was below 6% for both schizophrenia and healthy control samples at baseline and follow-up, with no significant diagnostic differences in the proportion with extreme deviations at either time point (p>0.05). For the schizophrenia group, infra-normal z-scores ranged 0-6.0% across regions at both time points (HC: 0-4.3%), and supra-normal z-scores ranged 0-5.4% (HC: 0-6.0%). The highest percentages of infra-normal deviance in schizophrenia were in superior temporal and superior frontal regions; supra-normal deviance was highest in occipital lobe and postcentral gyrus. Longitudinal findings: After FDR correction, there were no significant differences between diagnostic groups in longitudinal change (z-diff) in regional z-scores, indicating patients did not show progressive changes in morphometric similarity over time. No significant group differences were found for average cross-sectional total outlier count or change in total outlier count over time (p=0.64). The mean intra-group change in number of infra- or supra-normal regions was <1 for both groups. Clinical correlations: No significant correlations were observed between total PANSS scores and baseline z-scores (maximum r=0.14), nor between cross-sectional or change in outlier region count and IQ or PANSS scores. Comparison with raw data: The DMN finding was replicated using raw morphometric similarity values residualized for age, sex, Euler number, and scanner, but with a smaller effect size (d=-0.27, p<0.01) compared to normative modeling z-scores (d=-0.36, p<0.001), demonstrating that normative modeling improved statistical power.
Confidence Rating: High

clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa11_application_notes:
Answer: 1. First application of normative modeling to morphometric similarity and first longitudinal normative modeling study of this phenotype; 2. Morphometric similarity is increasingly recognized as biologically meaningful due to its association with underlying microstructural connectivity and cellular network structures forming axonal connections; 3. Normative modeling demonstrated increased statistical significance compared to traditional 'raw' data approaches for detecting DMN differences (d=-0.36 for z-scores vs d=-0.27 for raw values), supporting the value of normative modeling for capturing population patterns and clinical disparities while retaining ability to investigate individual differences; 4. The z-diff approach was implemented to assess longitudinal changes accounting for typical variation over time; 5. Replicability of morphometric similarity maps was demonstrated with good correspondence (Spearman ρ=0.8, p<0.001) between the 5-feature approach used in this study and the published 7-feature maps; 6. Sex-stratified supplemental analyses showed females had higher percentages of infra- and supra-normal deviance compared to males, with female schizophrenia patients showing infra-normal z-scores ranging 0-10.5% and supra-normal ranging 0-13.2% vs. males at 0-6.2% and 0-5.4% respectively; 7. The study established regional age-dependent normative trajectories showing mean regional morphometric similarity converges toward zero with increasing age; 8. Authors emphasize future research should integrate normative modeling with multimodal data (behavior, genetics, functional connectivity) for more comprehensive understanding of schizophrenia pathophysiology and individual variability; 9. Findings suggest morphometric similarity abnormalities in schizophrenia are not progressive over time in contrast to Alzheimer's disease where outlier counts track neurodegeneration, possibly reflecting a plateau after early illness stages or effects of treatment; 10. The increased morphometric similarity in the somatomotor network represents an underexplored finding that may reflect compensatory mechanisms.
Confidence Rating: High

Answer: 1. Training dataset diversity: While the study benefited from a substantial training set, larger and more heterogeneous datasets incorporating non-European ancestry data are needed for better population representation; 2. Training on healthy controls only: An alternative approach of including non-healthy individuals in the training set might increase model generalizability, though the study followed customary practices; 3. Regional independence assumption: The normative modeling framework treats each region as independent despite potential correlations among z-scores from neighboring regions (mitigation via PCA on z-scores suggested); 4. Lack of disease specificity: Normative models by definition can only detect deviations from the norm but not whether deviations are specific to a particular condition, limiting usefulness as a diagnostic biomarker (though could be part of a two-step classification procedure); 5. Network solution dependency: Findings only apply to the Yeo 7-network solution used to replicate prior work; alternative network parcellations may yield different results; 6. Clinical sample size: While comparable to previous normative modeling studies, larger multicenter clinical samples may enable identification of distinct patient clusters with significant deviance; 7. Variable explained variance: Explained variance differed among regions with some showing low variance, suggesting age-dependency varies considerably across regions, and morphometric similarity may be less sensitive to disease effects than cortical thickness or functional connectivity measures for some regions.

Supporting Text: This study has limitations. For clinical translation, progress in normative modeling stands as a crucial prerequisite, underscoring the necessity for a broadened diversification of datasets. While the present study benefited from a substantial training set, larger and more heterogeneous datasets, incorporating not solely European ancestry data, are imperative for a more accurate representation of the underlying population. An alternative strategy for normative modeling would be to include non-healthy individuals in the training set. This may increase the generalizability of the model. However, we followed customary practices by training the model on healthy controls only. The normative modeling framework employed herein treats each region as independent, notwithstanding potential correlations among z-scores from neighboring regions. To mitigate this challenge, one plausible strategy involves implementing data reduction techniques, such as principal component analysis applied to the z-scores. In addition, by definition, normative models can only detect deviations from the norm but not whether these are specific to a particular condition, thereby limiting their usefulness as a biomarker indicator. Of course, the normative modeling could be made part of a two-step procedure, where, in the second step, the z-scores and diagnostic labels are used as inputs for a classification algorithm. The classifier could be trained to discriminate between different disorders and would also indicate which regions are most important for this. We used the seven network solution as put forward by ref. 28 to replicate the findings by ref. 11. It must be recognized that our findings and those by ref. 11 only apply to this network solution and that alternative network solutions may provide different results. While our sample size of individuals with schizophrenia was comparable to previous normative modeling studies, larger (multicenter) clinical samples may enable the identification of distinct clusters of patients exhibiting significant deviance. [...] Furthermore, results must be interpreted with caution as the explained variance differed among regions, with some regions showing low variance, suggesting that age-dependency differs considerably among regions. Thus, while morphometric similarity has shown promise as a phenotype for identifying macroscopic brain abnormalities, our findings suggest that its utility in schizophrenia may be nuanced. Regional cortical thickness changes or functional connectivity alterations assessed through normative modeling may offer greater sensitivity to disease effects.

Replication study: This work explicitly aimed to replicate findings by Morgan et al. 2019 regarding cortical patterning of abnormal morphometric similarity in psychosis and DMN disruptions across functional networks; 2. Data availability: Study code and Docker container for normative modeling are available at https://github.com/iamjoostjanssen/NormModel_MorphoSim_SZ; publicly available datasets include AOMIC (OpenNeuro: ds003097, ds002785, ds002790), CamCAN, DLBS, IXI, Narratives (ds002345), OASIS3, NKI-Rockland, and SALD accessible via specified repositories; clinical Utrecht/GROUP data cannot be made publicly available; 3. Funding: Supported by multiple Spanish and European grants including Spanish Ministry of Science and Innovation, CIBER, European Union NextGenerationEU, Madrid Regional Government, EU Framework Programs, Innovative Medicines Initiative 2 (PRISM-2, AIMS-2-TRIALS, c4c), and NIH/NIMH awards (ProNET, FEP-CAUSAL, SZ-aging); 4. Follow-up interval: Mean time between scans was 3.95 years (SD 1.03) for healthy controls and 4.11 years (SD 0.95) for schizophrenia patients (Table 1A); 5. Clinical characteristics: Schizophrenia group showed mean age of onset 22.14 years (SD 5.28), baseline illness duration 6.41 years (SD 6.66), follow-up illness duration 11.08 years (SD 7.72); PANSS scores decreased from baseline to follow-up (total: 63.22→50.17; positive: 14.91→12.38; negative: 16.25→12.83; general: 31.15→24.97); 6. Scanner details: Two identical scanners were used for the longitudinal clinical dataset with all participants having baseline and follow-up scans on the same scanner; 7. Morphometric similarity computation: Used 5-feature approach (cortical thickness, surface area, cortical volume, mean curvature, Gaussian curvature) rather than 7-feature approach including DTI in prior work; 8. Network mapping: DKT atlas regions were mapped to seven Yeo functional networks based on maximum vertex overlap following Vasa et al. 2018 approach; 9. Model evaluation metrics reported: proportion of explained variance, mean standardized log loss (MSLL), standardized mean square error (SMSE), root mean square error (RMSE), Bayesian information criterion (BIC), rho (Pearson correlation), skewness, and kurtosis; Q-Q plots available on GitHub; 10. Global morphometric similarity: Supplemental analyses showed no statistically significant differences between diagnostic groups in global (whole-brain averaged) morphometric similarity at baseline (p=0.08) or follow-up (p=0.16); 12. ComBat harmonization: Supplement reports a sensitivity analysis using ComBat-corrected input to assess effect of scanner harmonization on replicability, showing the harmonized 5-features map was highly similar to non-harmonized map and the 7-features map from Morgan et al. 2019."
